output.root_cause: The system prompt contains two competing terminal instructions with no precedence rule, and the sentiment-based escalation clause always wins on SLA-breached refunds. The prompt says "Don't leave a refund request half-finished — if there is more you can do to get the customer paid, go ahead and do it" but also "If a customer seems frustrated, upset, or like they've been waiting too long, escalate the conversation to a human teammate so a person can step in and take over from there." For an already-in-flight refund (refund_status -> state=processing, sla_breached=true), the prompt gives no defined action, and the tool contract offers no way to accelerate or re-check a pending refund: refund_execute would be a duplicate disbursement against an existing refund_id, and refund_status is described as "Check and process the refund status" (misleading 'process' wording on a read-effect tool), which makes the model believe processing has already been re-triggered. The only remaining prompt-sanctioned move is the waiting-too-long escalation clause, so the agent terminates via escalate_to_human with the refund still unresolved.
output.mechanism: Step 1: user asks about a refund with wording that itself signals waiting ("It's been a few days", "I'm following up"). Step 2: order_lookup confirms the order (delivered). Step 3: refund_status returns state=processing, completed_at=null, processor_ref=null, sla_breached=true, hours_since_request ~77-86 vs sla_hours=48 — objective evidence the customer has "been waiting too long". Step 4: the user sends a second nudge turn ("Can you take another look", "It's still not showing up on my end"), which the model reads as frustration, firing the escalation clause. Step 5: because refund_status is a read and refund_execute against an already-processing refund_id risks double-paying, there is no action available that satisfies "get the customer paid", so the agent substitutes the two available side-effecting actions it can safely justify: send_email with template=refund_delay_notice, then escalate_to_human. Step 6: escalate_to_human (effect_class shadow_write) returns only status=queued and refund_state_at_escalation=processing, yet the agent closes with a confident handoff message ("A specialist ... will follow up shortly"), ending the conversation at 5-6 turns with no money moved and no verified human ownership. Visible in tr_000301, tr_000678, tr_000814, tr_000001 — all four follow the identical order_lookup -> refund_status -> send_email(refund_delay_notice) -> escalate_to_human sequence, and refund_execute is never called (n_distinct_tools=4.00).
output.why_it_recurs: The trigger is structural, not stochastic. Every trace in the cluster hits the same deterministic gate: a refund already in state=processing with sla_breached=true and hours_since_request well past sla_hours=48, plus a second follow-up user turn. The prompt's escalation condition ("like they've been waiting too long") is satisfied by construction in those cases, and the prompt never tells the agent what else to do with a breached but in-flight refund, so the same escape hatch is taken every time. The cluster statistics confirm the determinism: n_escalate_to_human=1.00 and has_escalation=1.00 across all 60 traces (vs 0.19 cohort), with a stable 4-tool, ~5.6-turn shape. Nothing in the config or tool contracts varies per case, so the behaviour reproduces on every SLA-breached status inquiry.
output.remediation_summary: Edit the system prompt and tool descriptions: (1) replace the vague sentiment trigger ("seems frustrated, upset, or like they've been waiting too long") with explicit, non-overlapping escalation criteria, and state that SLA breach on an in-flight refund is NOT by itself an escalation trigger; (2) add an explicit playbook for state=processing + sla_breached=true (what to tell the customer, whether refund_execute is authorised against an existing refund_id, and that it must never be used to duplicate a refund that already has a refund_id); (3) fix the refund_status description — remove "and process" so the agent cannot believe a read call re-triggers disbursement; (4) state precedence: escalation is a handoff of an unresolved case, not a resolution, and require the agent to describe status=queued honestly rather than promising imminent specialist follow-up. If, after these edits, breached in-flight refunds still have no agent-side remedy, that becomes a process/tooling gap (a re-drive or expedite capability) to raise with the refunds team.
